The Shang Dynasty. China's first historically confirmed civilization, the Shang ruled the Yellow River valley from approximately 1600 to 1046 BCE. Distinguished by sophisticated bronze casting, early writing systems, and oracle divination practices, the Shang established many foundations of Chinese culture that persisted for millennia. Their capital moved several times, with Anyang serving as the final administrative center. The Shang fell to the Zhou Dynasty, whose rulers justified their conquest through the concept of the Mandate of Heaven.

The Shang reigned approximately from 1600 to 1046 BCE, succeeding the legendary Xia Dynasty whose historicity remains debated. Archaeological evidence from sites like Anyang definitively confirms Shang existence, unlike earlier dynasties.

The Shang was ruled by a succession of kings. Early Shang history is obscured by legend, but later kings like Wu Ding are documented in oracle bones. Society was rigidly hierarchical with a king-priest at the apex, followed by nobility, merchants, artisans, farmers, and enslaved peoples.

The Shang were masters of bronze casting. They created ritual vessels, weapons, and chariots of unprecedented sophistication. Their bronze metallurgy represented such a technological leap that it defined the Bronze Age in China.

The Shang developed an early logographic writing system that evolved directly into modern Chinese characters. They used oracle bones—ox scapulae and tortoise shells—inscribed with questions, heated until cracked, then interpreted to divine royal will and divine approval.

The Shang deployed war chariots with bronze weapons and composite bows, giving unprecedented military advantage. They expanded territory through conquest and diplomacy and controlled much of the central Yellow River plain.

The Shang venerated Shang Di, the Lord on High, a supreme deity, alongside ancestor worship and nature spirits. They conducted elaborate sacrificial ceremonies, including human sacrifice, to secure favor with ancestors and deities.

The Shang Dynasty marks the threshold between prehistory and recorded history in China. Their oracle bones are humanity's earliest known systematic writing, and their bronze-casting techniques remained unmatched in the world for centuries. The Shang established the cosmological model of dynastic rule legitimized by heaven, a framework that Chinese dynasties would invoke for the next two thousand years. Their fall to the Zhou introduced the concept of the Mandate of Heaven, reframing dynastic succession from simple conquest into moral and cosmic necessity. Shang culture did not disappear; it was absorbed and elaborated by successive dynasties, making them foundational to all of Chinese civilization.
